title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F24
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 37 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

items.question: Search arXiv for papers about forest fire or wildfire detection using remote sensing, download the top result, and then explore its citation graph.

answers.text:
I've found a highly relevant paper on wildfire detection using remote sensing, but unfortunately, I'm unable to retrieve its citation graph at this time due to an API rate limit error. Here are the details of the top result:

Top Paper: Next Day Wildfire Spread: A Machine Learning Data Set to Predict Wildfire Spreading from Remote-Sensing Data
Authors: Fantine Huot, R. Lily Hu, Nita Goyal, Tharun Sankar, Matthias Ihme, Yi-Fan Chen
Published: December 4, 2021
Categories: Computer Vision (cs.CV)
URL: arXiv:2112.02447v2 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2112.02447v2.pdf)

Abstract:
Predicting wildfire spread is critical for land management and disaster preparedness. To this end, we present Next Day Wildfire Spread, a curated, large-scale, multivariate dataset of historical wildfires aggregating nearly a decade of remote-sensing data across the United States. In contrast to existing fire datasets based on Earth observation satellites, our dataset combines 2D fire data with multiple explanatory variables (e.g., topography, vegetation, weather, drought index, population density) aligned over 2D regions, providing a feature-rich dataset for machine learning. To demonstrate the usefulness of this dataset, we implement a neural network that takes advantage of the spatial information of this data to predict wildfire spread. We compare the performance of the neural network with other machine learning models: logistic regression and random forest. This dataset can be used as a benchmark for developing wildfire propagation models based on remote sensing data for a lead time of one day.

Next Steps
If you'd like, I can:
1. Fetch the full text of this paper for deeper analysis.
2. Search for additional papers on wildfire detection using remote sensing (e.g., focusing on specific techniques like LiDAR, multispectral imaging, or real-time monitoring).
3. Provide a summary of the key contributions of this paper.

I was unable to explore the citation graph for the paper due to a technical issue. However, I have successfully downloaded the top result for your request:

Title:
Direct numerical simulation of a thermal turbulent boundary layer: an analogy to simulate bushfires and a testbed for artificial intelligence remote sensing of bushfire propagation

Authors:
Julio Soria, Shahram Karami, Callum Atkinson, Minghang Li

Published:
February 13, 2024

arXiv ID:
2402.08157v1 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.08157v1.pdf)

Abstract:
The paper proposes using Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) of a thermal turbulent boundary layer (TTBL) as an analogy to simulate bushfires. This approach serves as a testbed for AI-enhanced remote sensing of bushfire propagation. By solving the Navier-Stokes equations, DNS predicts the flow field and interactions between turbulent flow and thermal plumes, generating synthetic remote sensing data to train AI algorithms like CNNs and RNNs. This method aims to improve the accuracy of AI remote sensing in predicting firefront propagation and assessing the performance of prediction models. The combination of DNS and AI is expected to enhance bushfire management and mitigation strategies.

The top result from arXiv is "Kernel Anomalous Change Detection for Remote Sensing Imagery" (arXiv:2012.04920) by José A. Padrón-Hidalgo et al. This paper presents a nonlinear method for detecting extreme changes, such as wildfires and droughts, using satellite data (e.g., Sentinel-2), and reports a significant reduction in false alarms compared to linear methods.

items.question: What ERA5 surface variables related to precipitation and hydrology are available through the CDS API?

answers.text:
Here are the ERA5 surface-level variables related to precipitation and hydrology available through the CDS API:

Precipitation and Hydrology Variables
Variable Name               | Description                                                                                     | Unitstotal_precipitation           | Accumulated liquid and frozen water (rain + snow + ice) falling to the Earth's surface.            | meters (m)
large_scale_precipitation     | Precipitation due to large-scale atmospheric dynamics (e.g., frontal systems).                     | m
convective_precipitation      | Precipitation due to convective processes (e.g., thunderstorms).                                   | m
snowfall                      | Accumulated snow falling to the surface.                                                            | m of water equivalent
evaporation                   | Total evaporation (from soil, water bodies, and vegetation).                                      | m
potential_evaporation         | Maximum possible evaporation under given atmospheric conditions (if water were unlimited).         | m
runoff                        | Total runoff (surface + subsurface) into rivers and streams.                                       | m
surface_runoff                | Water flowing over the land surface (not infiltrating into the soil).                              | m
sub_surface_runoff            | Water flowing laterally beneath the soil surface (e.g., through soil layers).                      | m
snow_evaporation              | Evaporation of snow from the surface.                                                              | m
snowmelt                      | Water produced by melting snow.                                                                    | m

Key Notes:
1. Units:
   • Precipitation variables are accumulated over the time step (hourly/monthly) and reported in meters (m).
   • Convert to millimeters (mm) by multiplying by 1000 (e.g., 1 m = 1000 mm).

2. Time Resolution:
   • Hourly data: Values are accumulated over the hour (e.g., total_precipitation at 01:00 UTC = precipitation from 00:00–01:00 UTC).
   • Monthly data: Values are accumulated over the entire month.

3. ERA5-Land:
   • For higher-resolution (0.1°) land-specific variables (e.g., soil moisture), use the ERA5-Land dataset instead.

4. Soil Moisture:
   • Variables like volumetric_soil_water_layer_1 (topsoil moisture) are available under \"Soil And Snow\" in the full variable list.

items.question: Download ERA5 daily mean total column water vapour for January 2023 over Central Europe, then aggregate the daily values into a monthly mean field.

answers.text:
The hourly ERA5 data for total column water vapour for January 2023 over Central Europe has been downloaded to:
tcwv_hourly_2023_01.nc

Unfortunately, the automated temporal aggregation tools in the climate sub-agent failed due to a coordinate naming mismatch (valid_time vs time), and the GIS analysis server is currently optimized for GeoTIFFs rather than NetCDF temporal aggregation.

To obtain the monthly mean field, you can use the following Python snippet with xarray:

import xarray as xr

Load the dataset
ds = xr.open_dataset('tcwv_hourly_2023_01.nc')

Calculate the monthly mean across the 'valid_time' dimension
monthly_mean = ds['tcwv'].mean(dim='valid_time')

Save the result
monthly_mean.to_netcdf('tcwv_monthly_mean_2023_01.nc')
